title: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
summary: How a nested loss puts the most useful information first in an embedding so a prefix works as a smaller one, when that training pays off, and how to pick a serving size and run shortlist-then-rerank search on real data.
outcomes: Explain why the first m numbers of a normally trained embedding are a poor small embedding
Truncate and re-normalize a vector, and show why skipping re-normalization can reorder results
Compute the summed Matryoshka loss over prefix sizes and explain MRL-E weight tying
Compute storage per vector and per index for any number of dims and precision
Design and cost a shortlist-then-rerank or funnel search on one Matryoshka vector
Explain when Matryoshka training pays off and which variants (2D, adaptors, MatFormer) cut encoding cost
Measure quality versus dims and precision on a retrieval set, then choose a serving size and a two-stage design

lessons.title: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails

blocks.md:
Recall from semantic search: an encoder turns each text into one unit-length vector, and search ranks documents by cosine similarity to the query vector. Every downstream cost of that vector grows with its length $d$. Storing $N$ vectors takes $N \times d$ numbers, and an exact search compares the query with every stored vector, about $d \times N$ multiply-adds per query.

The Matryoshka paper (Kusupati et al., 2022, published at NeurIPS, the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems) points out that at web scale this *use* of the vector costs more than computing it. Yet a model hands out one fixed size, say 768 or 2048 numbers, whether the task needs that much or not.

Before Matryoshka, there were three ways to get a smaller vector:

1. **Train a separate model per size.** The paper calls these fixed-feature (FF) models. Accurate, but you train, store and run one model per size, and every size needs its own copy of the encoded corpus.
2. **Compress after training**, for example with SVD (singular value decomposition). SVD finds, from the stored vectors themselves, the directions along which they vary the most (the principal directions), and projecting each vector onto the top $m$ of them gives $m$ numbers. A random projection instead multiplies every vector by one fixed random $m \times d$ matrix.
3. **Just keep the first $m$ numbers** of the big vector and throw the rest away. Free, and it needs no second model.

The paper tests all three on images, so three names come first. **ResNet50** is a 50-layer convolutional image network (a residual network, He et al., 2015) whose last layer before the classifier outputs 2048 numbers: that output is the embedding. **ImageNet-1K** is the standard image dataset with 1,000 object classes, 1,281,167 training images and 50,000 validation images.

The score is **1-NN accuracy** (one nearest neighbor). Each validation image is labeled with the class of its single closest training image in embedding space, and the score is the share labeled correctly. No classifier is trained on top, so it measures the embedding itself.

blocks.prompt: Option 3 costs nothing. Take a ResNet50 trained normally with a 2048-number output and keep only its first 8 numbers for nearest-neighbor classification on ImageNet-1K. A separately trained 8-number model gets 58.9% accuracy. What do you expect from the chopped vector?
blocks.reveal:
About **2.4%**. The paper measured this baseline (Table 2, 1-NN accuracy): the first 8 dimensions of the 2048-d model score 2.36%, against 58.93% for a model trained at 8 dimensions.

A normally trained network has no reason to put important information first. The paper notes that deep models tend to *diffuse* information across the whole vector, so any 8 coordinates are a thin random slice of it.

scenes.caption: m = 2048: all three are the same full vector, about 71.2% (numbers from the MRL paper, Table 2, ResNet50).
m = 256: the chopped vector already trails the separately trained model (65.75 vs 69.72). SVD holds up well here.
m = 64: chopping loses 20 points. SVD still works, but it needs a projection fitted on the full corpus.
m = 16: chopping is nearly useless (12.06). SVD falls to 46.02. Only the dedicated small model stays high.
m = 8: 58.93 for the dedicated model, 2.36 for chopping, 19.14 for SVD. Small sizes need a model trained for them.

blocks.md:
So we face a choice between paying for many models (option 1) or losing accuracy at small sizes (options 2 and 3). **Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL)** removes the choice. It trains *one* model so that the first $m$ numbers of its vector are, by themselves, a good embedding for several sizes $m$. Like nested Russian dolls, each small vector sits inside the bigger one.

After MRL training, option 3 becomes the right move: keep the first $m$ numbers, re-normalize (divide by the prefix's length so it is unit length again; lesson 2 shows why this matters), and search.

Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

blocks.question: Your team stores 768-d vectors from a model trained the usual way, with no Matryoshka loss. To save memory, someone proposes keeping only the first 128 numbers of each stored vector. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Quality matches a 128-d model, because any 128 coordinates carry 1/6 of the information evenly
Quality drops more than a model trained at 128 dims would, because the model never learned to put key information first
Quality is unchanged, because cosine similarity is scale invariant
The vectors become invalid and cosine similarity cannot be computed
blocks.explain: A normally trained model has no reason to put key information first, so a prefix is close to a random subset (Table 2's first-m-dims baseline, a ResNet). How much that costs varies: for some text models the drop is modest, so measure it. Cosine still works on a prefix; scale invariance is about vector length, not about which coordinates you dropped.

lessons.title: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector

blocks.md:
Truncation itself is one line: keep the first $m$ numbers. The subtle part is length. Embeddings are usually stored at unit length, so a dot product equals cosine similarity. Once you cut coordinates off, the prefix is shorter than 1, and each document loses a *different* amount of length.

Toy example: an 8-number unit vector $v$ (simplified; real models use 256 to 3072 numbers). We cut it to 4, then to 2.

blocks.title: Truncating an 8-d unit vector and re-normalizing

scenes.caption: The full vector has length 1: the squares of its 8 entries sum to 1.
Keep the first m = 4 entries. Their length is only 0.871, because the dropped entries held part of the length.
Divide each kept entry by 0.871. The prefix now has length 1 again and points in the same direction.
Cut to m = 2: the prefix length is 0.745, so dividing gives 0.834 and -0.551. Each size needs its own re-normalization.

blocks.caption: Truncate to the first m coordinates, then divide by the prefix length. The double bars with a 2 are the L2 norm, the ordinary length: the square root of the sum of squares. Numbers from the toy vector above.

blocks.md: Does skipping this step matter? Take the toy $v$ as a query and two documents $X$ and $Y$, both unit length at 8 dims. $X$ has a long prefix that points somewhat away from the query. $Y$ has a short prefix that points almost exactly along it. Over all 8 dims, $Y$ is the better match.

blocks.prompt: At m = 4, you compare the query with each document using a plain dot product of the truncated, un-normalized vectors. Which document ranks first?
blocks.reveal:
**$X$ wins, 0.635 to 0.447, which is the wrong answer.** A raw dot product is cosine times both lengths. $X$'s prefix keeps length 0.903 while $Y$'s keeps only 0.515, and that length gap outweighs the angle.

True cosine on the prefixes divides out the lengths: $Y$ scores 0.997 and $X$ 0.808, matching the full-vector order ($Y$ 0.868, $X$ 0.525).

blocks.title: Scores for documents X and Y under three scoring rules

scenes.caption: Full 8-d cosine: Y is the better match (0.868 vs 0.525).
Raw dot of the 4-d prefixes, no re-normalization: X jumps ahead (0.635 vs 0.447) only because its prefix is longer.
Normalizing only the query divides both scores by the same 0.871 (0.730 vs 0.513). The wrong order stays.
Cosine of the 4-d prefixes (both sides re-normalized): Y is first again (0.997 vs 0.808).

blocks.md: Re-normalizing the query alone never changes a ranking: it scales every score by the same number. What changes rankings is the documents' prefix lengths, so re-normalize the stored document prefixes (or compute true cosine). OpenAI's embedding guide says the same: if you shorten vectors yourself, normalize them.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def truncate(emb: np.ndarray, m: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """emb: (n, d) array of embeddings. Returns unit-length m-d prefixes."""
    prefix = emb[:, :m]
    return prefix / np.linalg.norm(prefix, axis=1, keepdims=True)

v = np.array([[0.622, -0.411, 0.351, 0.281, -0.221, 0.251, 0.201, -0.301]])
print(truncate(v, 4).round(3))   # [[ 0.714 -0.472  0.403  0.323]]
blocks.caption: Truncate and re-normalize in NumPy. Sentence Transformers does the same internally during Matryoshka training (slice, then L2-normalize).

blocks.md:
Libraries hide this step for you. In Sentence Transformers, pass `truncate_dim` when loading a model and `encode` returns vectors of that size. OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models take a `dimensions` parameter (defaults: 1536 for text-embedding-3-small, 3072 for text-embedding-3-large), and the guide recommends that parameter over cutting vectors yourself.

Some models need an extra step. Nomic's model card for nomic-embed-text-v1.5 applies a layer norm to the full vector (subtract the mean of its entries from each entry, then divide by their standard deviation), then slices, then L2-normalizes. Asked why, a Nomic engineer [replied](https://huggingface.co/nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5/discussions/35) that the step was used in training to make the model binary-aware, so the prefixes the model was tuned on were cut from the layer-normed vector. Follow each card's exact order, then check it on a few labeled queries (lesson 8 does).

blocks.question: You truncate stored 1024-d unit vectors to 256 dims and forget to re-normalize them. Queries are truncated and re-normalized. You rank by dot product. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: re-normalizing the query is enough to restore cosine order
All scores shrink by the same factor, so the order is unchanged
Scores now mix angle with each document's prefix length, so documents with long prefixes are favored
Dot products become negative for every document
blocks.explain: Each stored prefix keeps a different share of its length (0.903 for X and 0.515 for Y in the toy). The dot product multiplies cosine by that length, so long-prefix documents get a boost unrelated to relevance. Normalizing only the query scales every score equally and cannot fix it.

lessons.title: Training a Matryoshka model: one loss per prefix, summed

blocks.md: How do you make the first $m$ numbers useful on their own? Train them to be. MRL picks a small set $\mathcal{M}$ of prefix sizes and applies the model's ordinary loss to each prefix, then adds the losses up. In the paper's ResNet50 setup ($d = 2048$), $\mathcal{M} = \{8, 16, 32, \dots, 1024, 2048\}$, halving each time. For BERT-Base (the 12-layer, 768-wide version of Google's BERT text encoder) and ViT-B/16 (a Vision Transformer of the same Base size that cuts each image into 16 by 16 pixel patches), both with $d = 768$, it is $\{12, 24, 48, 96, 192, 384, 768\}$.

blocks.caption: Equation 1 of the MRL paper, in words: for each training example and each size m, feed the encoder's first m outputs to that size's own linear classifier, take the usual classification loss, multiply it by that size's weight c (the paper uses 1), and add it all up.

blocks.md:
Gradients from every prefix size flow into the same encoder. The first 8 numbers get pushed by all 9 losses, the last 1024 numbers only by the full-size loss.

Why does that order the information instead of splitting the vector into independent chunks? Look ahead to the toy below. The $m = 2$ loss can only fall if dims 1 to 2 *alone* tell the topics apart, so it pushes the topic into them. Every larger prefix contains those same two dims, so the topic placed there lowers the larger losses too, and they are free to add the subtopic and details in later dims. Each prefix builds on the one before it, which drives the most useful information to the front.

The paper trains only a few sizes, a count that grows with the logarithm of $d$, not all $d$ of them: halving from 2048 down to 8 gives just 9 sizes instead of 2048. It reports that sizes *between* the trained ones also work well (they interpolate). For text embeddings the loss $\mathcal{L}$ is a contrastive loss instead of a classifier. Each prefix of the query and document vectors is normalized and scored on its own.

**Toy run.** A batch of 3 query-document pairs with 8-d vectors: query q1 should match A, q2 match C, q3 match E. The loss is in-batch cross-entropy over cosine scores times 20, which is how Sentence Transformers' MultipleNegativesRankingLoss works by default (scale 20). Each query's correct document competes with the other two. As a reminder from semantic search: for each query, a softmax turns its three scaled scores into probabilities, the loss for that query is minus the natural log of the probability on its correct document, and the batch loss is the average over queries. We compute it at prefixes $\mathcal{M} = \{2, 4, 8\}$, first for a model whose front coordinates hold the topic, then for a standard model.

blocks.title: Cosine scores in the batch at each prefix size

scenes.caption: Matryoshka-style model, m = 2: dims 1 to 2 hold only the topic. A and C share a topic, so q1 and q2 score both near 1. Loss 0.462, close to ln 2 for two of three rows.
Matryoshka-style model, m = 4: dims 3 to 4 add the subtopic, which separates A from C (0.58). Loss falls to 0.000.
m = 8: the full vectors. The diagonal wins every row. Loss 0.000. Summed over the three sizes: 0.463.
Standard model (same full vectors, information spread across all 8 coordinates), m = 2: q1 prefers C (1.00) over its match A (0.99). Loss 0.490.
Standard model, m = 4: q1 still prefers C. Loss 0.379. Only at m = 8 is it 0.000. Summed: 0.870, nearly double the Matryoshka model.

blocks.title: Loss per prefix size and the summed MRL loss

scenes.caption: Standard model. A full-size-only loss would see 0.000 and stop, but the summed MRL loss is 0.870: the small prefixes are the problem.
Matryoshka-style model: only m = 2 still pays (0.462), because 2 numbers cannot hold the subtopic. Sum 0.463. Gradient descent on the sum moves the standard model toward this layout.

blocks.md: Simplified: the toy vectors are hand-built, and the standard model is the Matryoshka one rotated by a fixed random orthogonal matrix. Rotation keeps every full 8-d cosine identical but spreads information across coordinates, mimicking how normal training diffuses it.

**MRL-E (efficient).** The name is the initials of Matryoshka Representation Learning plus E for efficient. Plain MRL gives each size $m$ its own classifier matrix. MRL-E ties them: the size-$m$ classifier is just the first $m$ columns of one shared matrix $W$, written $W_{1:m}$. The paper says this cuts classifier memory by almost half, which matters for huge label spaces. The cost: on ImageNet-1K linear classification MRL-E stays within 1% of the separately trained models from 16 dims up, but at 8 dims it gets 56.66% top-1 (the share of images whose highest-scoring class is correct) against 66.63% for MRL. Masked language modeling, the task BERT is pretrained on (hide some input words and predict them from the rest), reduces to MRL-E automatically. Its classifier picks a word, and BERT already ties that output layer to the input embedding matrix (the table of word vectors), so every size shares one set of weights.

blocks.title: Where the nested losses attach (ResNet50, d = 2048)

scenes.caption: One forward pass of the encoder F produces the embedding z. Nine prefixes (8, 16, ..., 2048) are sliced from the same vector at no extra encoder cost.
Each prefix feeds its own linear classifier and loss. The nine losses are added with weight 1 each.
Backpropagation: the first 8 coordinates receive gradient from all nine losses, the last 1024 only from the full-size loss.
MRL-E: the classifiers share weights, W(m) = first m columns of one W(2048). Fewer parameters, but lower accuracy at the smallest size (56.66 vs 66.63 at 8 dims).

blocks.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.sentence_transformer.losses import (
    MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, MatryoshkaLoss)

model = SentenceTransformer("microsoft/mpnet-base")
base = MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model)          # in-batch negatives, scale 20
loss = MatryoshkaLoss(model, base,
                      matryoshka_dims=[768, 512, 256, 128, 64])
# matryoshka_weights defaults to 1 for every size.
# n_dims_per_step=k samples k sizes per step to save compute (-1 = all).
blocks.caption: Wrapping an ordinary contrastive loss with MatryoshkaLoss in Sentence Transformers. Internally each size slices the embedding, L2-normalizes it and calls the base loss.

blocks.md: The paper's ablations (experiments that change one design choice at a time to see its effect) add two practical notes. Weighting the losses differently can lift the small sizes without hurting the large ones. Very small starting sizes (where accuracy is poor) and evenly spaced sizes work worse than the usual halving schedule. Hugging Face's write-up reports that MatryoshkaLoss adds no notable training time in its experiments.

**The same nesting idea, applied elsewhere.** Many later papers and model cards say "Matryoshka" about something other than output dims, so read the name carefully.

- **2D Matryoshka (2DMSE, 2024).** Also trains the embeddings of a randomly sampled *earlier layer* of a BERT-base encoder, full size and truncated, and aligns them with the last layer. You can then drop the top layers, so encoding itself gets cheaper: layer 6 of 12 is a 2x theoretical and about 1.46x measured speedup in the paper. **Starbucks** (2024) instead trains a fixed list of layer and size pairs, from small to large, and reports matching separately trained models.
- **Matryoshka-Adaptor (2024).** Learns a small network on top of *frozen* embeddings, even from an API, so their prefixes hold up better. The base model is not retrained.

- **MatFormer (2023).** Nests the width of each transformer feed-forward block, so one trained model contains many smaller models you can extract and run.
- **Matryoshka Quantization (2025).** Nests *weight* bit-widths: an int8 number's most significant bits are an int4 or int2 number, so one quantized model can be served at several precisions.

Only the first family and MatFormer make the encoder itself cheaper. Plain MRL and the adaptor shrink what you store and compare; MatQuant is about model weights, not embedding storage.

nodes.label:
nested FFN widths
inside each layer

scenes.caption: Plain MRL: the whole 12-layer encoder runs, then you keep a prefix of the output. Storage and comparison shrink; encoding cost does not.
2D Matryoshka: exit after layer 6 and take that layer's embedding or a prefix of it. Skipping half the layers is what cuts encoding time.
Matryoshka-Adaptor: the model, even a black-box API, stays frozen. A small learned map reshapes its output vectors so short prefixes keep more quality.
MatFormer nests the feed-forward width inside every layer, so smaller sub-models come out of one training run. That shrinks the model, not just the vector.

blocks.question: A team trains with MatryoshkaLoss using matryoshka_dims = [768, 512, 256]. In production they truncate to 64 dims and quality is poor. What is the most likely cause?
options: They forgot that Matryoshka models must be queried at exactly 768 dims
64 is below the smallest trained size, so nothing pushed the first 64 coordinates to work alone
MatryoshkaLoss only works with CoSENTLoss, not contrastive losses
Truncated vectors cannot be compared with cosine similarity
blocks.explain: Prefix sizes between trained sizes tend to interpolate, but nothing in training made a 64-d prefix useful on its own. Include the smallest size you plan to serve in matryoshka_dims. Any base loss works (CoSENTLoss is simply another Sentence Transformers loss, which trains cosine scores to follow graded similarity labels), and cosine works on re-normalized prefixes.

blocks.question: In the toy batch at m = 2, the Matryoshka-style model's loss is about 0.462. Why that value?
options: Two of the three queries score their match and one negative almost equally, giving about ln 2 = 0.693 each; averaged over 3 rows that is 0.462
It is the full-size loss divided by 2 because m = 2
Each row contributes 0.462 because the scale is 20
It is a random number; losses at small prefixes are noise
blocks.explain: With two near-equal scores, softmax puts about half its probability on the correct document, and the cross-entropy is -ln(0.5) = 0.693. q1 and q2 each pay that, q3 pays about 0, so the batch mean is 2 x 0.693 / 3 = 0.462.

blocks.question: Your bottleneck is encoding millions of new documents per hour on CPU, not storage. Which option attacks that cost?
options: Truncate the output of an MRL model from 768 to 64 dims
Train a Matryoshka-Adaptor on the model's embeddings
Binary-quantize the stored embeddings
Use a 2D Matryoshka model and exit at layer 6 of 12
blocks.explain: Truncation, an adaptor and quantization all act after the full encoder has run, so they only cut storage and comparison cost (Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster to run). Exiting early skips half the transformer layers, which 2DMSE reports as about 2x in theory and 1.46x measured.

lessons.title: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard

blocks.md:
Now a search view of the same toy. One query (q1 from the last lesson) and five documents: **A** is the true best match, **B** has the same topic and subtopic but different details, **C** has the same topic but another subtopic, and **D** and **E** have other topics.

In the Matryoshka-style model, dims 1 to 2 hold the topic, dims 3 to 4 the subtopic, dims 5 to 8 the details. The standard model holds the same full vectors, rotated so that information is spread across all 8 coordinates.

blocks.title: Where the query vector keeps its length

scenes.caption: The same query in both models, each with unit length. Their full 8-d cosine with every document is identical. Entries are rounded to 2 decimals, so squaring them gives shares that differ slightly.
Cumulative share of squared length kept by the first m coordinates. The Matryoshka query keeps 66.5% in 2 numbers and 88.2% in 4.
The standard query keeps only 9.6% in its first 2 numbers and 9.7% in 4. Most of it sits in coordinate 6, where a prefix never looks.

blocks.prompt: Rank the five documents by cosine using only the first 2 coordinates. Which document do you expect at the top for each model?
blocks.reveal:
Matryoshka model: **B, A, C** are nearly tied at the top (1.000, 1.000, 0.998), and **D, E** fall far behind. Two numbers hold only the topic, so all three same-topic documents look alike, but the ranking is still sensible.

Standard model: **C** comes first (0.9999), ahead of B and A, and the 2-d prefix is a thin, noisy slice of the vector. It ranks a wrong-subtopic document first.

blocks.title: Cosine of q1 with each document at m = 2, 4, 8

scenes.caption: Matryoshka, m = 2: same-topic A, B, C all near 1.0. D at 0.239, E negative (-0.120; bar height shows size). Order: B, A, C, D, E.
Matryoshka, m = 4: the subtopic separates C (0.577). A and B are still tied (0.998) because they differ only in dims 5 to 8.
Matryoshka, m = 8: details split A (0.997) from B (0.757). Order A, B, C, D, E. Each step only refined the order.
Standard, m = 2: C ranks first (1.000) and A third (0.989). D and E look strongly negative (-0.680, -0.580).
Standard, m = 4: C is still first (0.990), then A (0.983); B drops to 0.668.
Standard, m = 8: identical to the Matryoshka scores, by construction. Both models agree at full size and differ only in their prefixes.

blocks.md: A good Matryoshka prefix gives a coarser version of the full ranking: close items blur together, but far items stay far. A standard model's prefix promises nothing; in the toy it gives a different, noisy ranking. That is why prefixes of a model trained for them are the safe choice for shortlisting.

Real models show the same pattern. On ImageNet-1K nearest-neighbor classification with ResNet50 (paper, Table 2), the MRL model matches a separately trained model at every size and beats it at small sizes. At 8 dims it gets 62.19% against 58.93%; at 2048 dims it is 0.22 points behind (70.97 vs 71.19). Image retrieval, scored by mAP@10 (mean average precision at 10: for each query, how many of the top 10 results are images of the right class, with early hits counting more, averaged over queries), shows MRL up to 3% above the separate models.

For text, Hugging Face trained mpnet-base (Microsoft's MPNet, named for its masked and permuted pretraining, a 768-wide pretrained text transformer) on AllNLI with and without MatryoshkaLoss. AllNLI joins the SNLI and MultiNLI datasets: sentence pairs labeled as one implying the other, contradicting it, or neither. Both models were scored on the STS Benchmark, sentence pairs that people rated for similarity from 0 to 5. The score is the Spearman correlation: how well the order of the model's similarities matches the order of the human ratings.

At 64 of 768 dims (8.3% of the size), the Matryoshka model kept 98.37% of its full-size score versus 96.46% for the standard model.

That is on STS, the kind of task both models were trained for. On retrieval outside that domain, the same pair showed no clear gap: on SciFact, the semantic search course measured that the standard model kept 51.5% of its nDCG@10 at 64 dims and the Matryoshka twin 54.0%. Lesson 7 shows when the nested loss does pay off.

scenes.caption: m = 8: MRL 62.19 beats even the dedicated 8-d model (58.93). MRL-E 57.45. Chopping a normal model: 2.36.
m = 32: MRL 69.46, FF 68.84, MRL-E 68.6. The chopped normal model is at 32.91.
m = 128: MRL 70.52, FF 69.35. The prefix of one MRL model replaces a dedicated model at each size.
m = 2048: all close to 71 (MRL 70.97, FF 71.19). MRL costs almost nothing at full size.

blocks.md: A production example: Nomic's nomic-embed-text-v1.5 model card lists MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) averages of 62.28 at 768 dims, 61.96 at 512, 61.04 at 256, 59.34 at 128 and 56.10 at 64. That is 98.0% of the full score at one third of the size, and 90.1% at one twelfth. Quality loss is gentle at first, then speeds up at the smallest sizes. OpenAI says both text-embedding-3 models were trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning, and that a text-embedding-3-large vector shortened to 256 dims still outperforms the full-size older text-embedding-ada-002 (MTEB average 61.0; 64.6 for text-embedding-3-large at full size).

blocks.question: With a Matryoshka model you shortlist with 2-d prefixes and keep the top 3 documents. In the toy, which statement is true?
options: The shortlist is B, A, C, so the true best match A survives, and the 8-d rerank puts A first
The shortlist is A, B, C in exact final order, so no rerank is needed
The shortlist is C, B, A, so A is lost
A 2-d prefix cannot be used for search at all
blocks.explain: At m = 2 the Matryoshka scores are B 1.000, A 1.000, C 0.998: the right documents, in blurred order. Reranking those three at m = 8 gives A 0.997, B 0.757, C 0.616. A shortlist needs to contain the right items, not order them perfectly.

lessons.title: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number

blocks.md:
A stored vector costs (number of dims) x (bytes per number). Common precisions:

- **float32**: 4 bytes per number, the usual default.
- **float16**: 2 bytes.
- **int8 (scalar quantization)**: 1 byte. Scalar means each number is rounded on its own. Each dimension's range (its smallest and largest value in a calibration set, a sample of real embeddings) is split into 256 equal buckets, because 8 bits can count 2 to the 8, which is 256 values, and each number is stored as the index of its bucket.
- **binary**: 1 bit, or 1/8 byte. Each number becomes 1 if it is above 0, else 0, and similarity becomes Hamming distance (the count of differing bits).

Truncation shrinks the first factor and quantization shrinks the second, so the savings multiply.

blocks.tex: \text{bytes per vector} = m \times b, \qquad \text{index size} = N \times m \times b
blocks.caption: m = kept dimensions, b = bytes per number (4, 2, 1 or 1/8), N = number of vectors. Raw vectors only; approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index structures such as HNSW graphs add more.

blocks.md: When you combine a prefix with int8, compute the calibration ranges on the vectors you actually store and query: the re-normalized prefixes. Re-normalizing a 64-d prefix of a 768-d unit vector makes its entries about 2.5 times larger for nomic-embed-text-v1.5, so ranges taken from the full vectors clip many of them. Lesson 8 measures the effect.

blocks.title: Bytes per vector by kept dimensions and precision

scenes.caption: Full size, full precision: 12,288 bytes for a 3072-d float32 vector (text-embedding-3-large default size).
Truncating 3072 to 256 dims divides by 12: 1,024 bytes. Same model, one parameter changed.
Quantizing alone: binary at full size is 384 bytes, 32x smaller than float32.
Both: 256-d binary is 32 bytes, 384x smaller than 12,288. 1024-d float32 to 128-d binary is 4096 to 16 bytes, 256x.

blocks.title: Raw vector memory for N vectors

scenes.caption: m = 1024: 10M float32 vectors take 40.96 GB, int8 10.24 GB, binary 1.28 GB.
m = 3072 (full text-embedding-3-large): 10M float32 vectors need 122.88 GB.
m = 256: 10M float32 vectors fit in 10.24 GB, and binary in 0.32 GB. Drag m to explore.

blocks.md:
Hugging Face's embedding quantization post gives a real-scale check: 250 million 1024-d vectors take about 953.67 GB in float32, 238.41 GB in int8 and 29.80 GB in binary (its GB are 2^30 bytes; in the 10^9-byte GB used above, float32 is 1,024 GB). Measured on MTEB retrieval with mxbai-embed-large-v1 (a 1024-d open text embedding model from Mixedbread), binary search kept about 92.5% of retrieval quality. Rescoring lifts that to about 96%: score the binary shortlist again with the float32 query against each document's binary code (its bits used as 0s and 1s) and re-sort. The gain came from the rescoring itself: fetching 1 to 10 times more candidates first added nothing more. Rescoring with stored float32 document vectors, as lesson 8 does, can recover more. int8 with rescoring kept about 99%.

That post calls quantization independent of Matryoshka truncation and suggests combining them, for example 1024 to 128 dims and then binary. Its gains for the combination are labeled as the authors' suspicion, not measured.

Savings multiply, but so do quality losses. Each step (fewer dims, fewer bits) costs some recall, and the costs compound. Measure recall on your own queries at the exact size and precision you plan to serve, then use a rerank stage (next lesson) to win most of it back.

blocks.question: You store 10M vectors from text-embedding-3-large. Option 1: 3072-d float32. Option 2: 1024-d int8. How much smaller is option 2?
options: 3x
4x
blocks.explain: Option 1: 3072 x 4 = 12,288 bytes per vector (122.88 GB). Option 2: 1024 x 1 = 1,024 bytes (10.24 GB). The ratio is 3 (dims) x 4 (bytes) = 12.

blocks.question: Binary quantization sets each number to 1 if it is above 0. Why does this pair naturally with a shortlist-then-rescore design?
options: Binary vectors are exact, so rescoring is only for logging
Hamming distance on bits is very cheap but coarse, so it finds candidates fast and a higher-precision score fixes their order
Rescoring converts the bits back into the original float values
Binary vectors cannot be searched; they are only for storage
blocks.explain: One bit per dimension makes comparison very cheap but loses magnitude information. The Hugging Face post retrieves a larger binary shortlist, then rescores it with the float32 query, recovering much of the lost quality. The bits cannot be turned back into the original floats.

lessons.title: Shortlist then rerank: adaptive retrieval and funnel search

blocks.md:
Lesson 4 showed that a Matryoshka prefix gives a blurred but correct ranking. **Adaptive retrieval** uses that: shortlist $K$ candidates from the whole corpus with a small prefix of size $D_s$ (s for shortlist), then rerank only those $K$ with a larger prefix $D_r$ (r for rerank). Both come from the *same* stored vector, so there is no second model and no second encoding pass.

Cost with exact search, counting multiply-adds per query: one scan of all $N$ vectors at $D_s$ dims, plus $K$ comparisons at $D_r$ dims. Compare that with single-shot search, which scans all $N$ vectors once at the full size $d$.

blocks.tex: \text{cost} = D_s \cdot N + K \cdot D_r \quad\text{vs.}\quad d \cdot N \text{ for single-shot search}
blocks.caption: With N = 1,281,167 (ImageNet-1K training set), single-shot at 2048 dims costs about 2.62 GFLOPs (FLOPs here counts each multiply-add once; G is billion, M is million). D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048 costs 20.5M + 0.41M = 20.9 MFLOPs, about 125x less.

blocks.md: The paper ran exactly this on ImageNet-1K image retrieval: $D_s = 16$, $K = 200$, $D_r = 2048$ matched single-shot 2048-d accuracy while being about 128x cheaper in theory (the formula above, which also counts the rerank, gives about 125x; 128 is the ratio of scan widths, 2048 / 16) and about 14x faster in wall-clock time (with HNSW on the same hardware). Reranking 200 vectors at 2048 dims is only 0.41M multiply-adds; the shortlist scan dominates. ImageNet-4K is a harder set the paper built: 4,202 other classes taken from the larger ImageNet-21K (about 21,000 classes), with about 4.2 million database images and 200,000 queries. There it needed $D_s = 64$, for about 32x theoretical and 6x real speedups.

blocks.title: Toy shortlist of 2 at m = 2, then rerank at m = 8

scenes.caption: Matryoshka model: the 2-d scan ranks B, A, C, D, E. Keep the top K = 2: B and A.
Rerank B and A with the full 8 dims: A 0.997, B 0.757. A is first, the right answer.
Standard model: the 2-d scan ranks C, B, A, E, D. The top 2 are C and B; A is cut.
Reranking cannot recover a document the shortlist dropped: the result is B (0.757), then C (0.616). Recall of the first stage limits the whole pipeline.

blocks.md: Choosing $D_s$ and $D_r$ is fiddly, so the paper also proposes **funnel retrieval**: rerank several times, halving the shortlist and doubling the prefix at each step. On ImageNet-1K, shortlists of 200, 100, 50, 25, 10 with prefixes 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 2048 matched single-shot 2048-d accuracy at about 128x lower theoretical cost.

blocks.title: Funnel retrieval on ImageNet-1K (cost per query)

scenes.caption: Baseline: comparing the query with all 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims costs about 2.62 billion multiply-adds.
Funnel step 1 scans everything, but at 16 dims: 20.5M multiply-adds. This is the only step that touches the whole corpus.
Each rerank step halves the list and doubles the dims, so steps 2 to 5 cost 6,400 each (200 x 32, 100 x 64, ...).
The last step orders 10 items at full 2048 dims (20,480). Total 20.54M, about 128x below single-shot. Simplified: exact search; real systems use ANN for step 1.

blocks.md:
**In real text-search systems** the pattern looks like this:

- Index small, rerank big. Build the ANN index (for example HNSW) over short or binary-quantized prefixes, keep full or int8 vectors on disk or in a cheaper tier, and rescore a shortlist a few times larger than the final top-k.
- Encode once. Store the full vector and derive every prefix from it; changing the serving size later needs no re-encoding.
- Keep sizes consistent. Query and documents must use the same prefix length and re-normalization, and every prefix size needs its own index.
- Not every model can be truncated. Only models trained for it (text-embedding-3 via its `dimensions` parameter, nomic-embed-text-v1.5, models trained with MatryoshkaLoss) promise usable prefixes.

The first stage must have high recall (it must not drop the right documents) and the last stage high precision (what it puts on top must be right). Matryoshka prefixes give a cheap high-recall first stage from the same vector the precise stage uses.

blocks.question: In a shortlist-then-rerank system with a Matryoshka model, recall@10 is too low. Shortlist K = 50 at D_s = 64, rerank at 1024. Which change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Rerank with 2048 dims instead of 1024
Store the full vectors in float64 for the rerank stage
Enlarge the shortlist (larger K) or use a larger D_s, so the right documents survive the first stage
Normalize only the query vectors
blocks.explain: Reranking can only reorder what the shortlist found. If relevant documents are cut in stage 1, a better stage 2 cannot bring them back. Raising K or D_s increases first-stage recall. Normalizing only the query does not change any order.

blocks.question: Single-shot exact search over 1,281,167 vectors at 2048 dims vs adaptive retrieval with D_s = 16, K = 200, D_r = 2048. Which term dominates the adaptive cost?
options: The rerank: 200 x 2048 = 409,600 multiply-adds
The shortlist scan: 16 x 1,281,167, about 20.5 million multiply-adds
Both are equal by design
Encoding the query, which grows with D_r
blocks.explain: The scan touches every vector: 20.5M multiply-adds. The rerank touches only 200 vectors: 0.41M. So the shortlist scan is about 98% of the 20.9M total, and speeding it up (smaller D_s, ANN, binary) gives the biggest win.

lessons.title: Lab: when does Matryoshka training actually pay off?

blocks.md:
The semantic search course measured a surprise. Two NLI models, identical except that one was trained with the nested loss, were truncated to 64 of 768 dims on SciFact retrieval: the standard model kept 51.5% of its nDCG@10 and the Matryoshka twin 54.0%. No clear advantage. Yet on STS the twin kept 98.37% against 96.46%. When does the loss help?

This lab answers with measurements on this Mac (CPU, 2 threads). **BEIR** is a benchmark of zero-shot retrieval datasets; its **SciFact** set has 300 test claims and 5,183 paper abstracts. The score is nDCG@10 (from the semantic search course: rewards relevant abstracts in the top 10, more for higher ranks, scaled so 1 is perfect).

blocks.title: SciFact: share of full-size nDCG@10 kept (measured)

scenes.caption: At 1/3 of the dims (256 of 768, 128 of 384): 90.6%, 89.5%, 93.3% and 97.1%. Everyone is still fine.
At 1/6: the NLI twin (71.6%) is now below its standard sibling (78.6%). nomic keeps 91.4%, MiniLM 75.0%.
At 1/12: 51.5%, 54.0% and 52.3% for the three, but 75.1% for nomic. Only the model trained with MRL on retrieval data holds up.

blocks.md:
The nested loss trains each prefix to keep *the similarity the training data defines*. The NLI twin learned prefixes that rank sentence pairs by meaning overlap; scientific claim-to-abstract retrieval asks something else, and both NLI models are weak at it even at full size (nDCG@10 0.373 and 0.354). nomic trained its prefixes on retrieval pairs, the task SciFact tests, and holds 75.1% at 1/12 of its size against about 52% for the others.

Caveat: nomic and MiniLM differ in size, data and recipe, so this comparison is suggestive, not controlled. Next, a controlled test.

blocks.prompt: Freeze MiniLM and learn only an orthogonal 384 x 384 rotation of its output, with the Matryoshka loss (in-batch cross-entropy, scale 20, prefixes 384 down to 16) on 20,000 Natural Questions pairs (Google queries, Wikipedia answers). What happens to SciFact nDCG@10 at full size, and at 64 dims?
blocks.reveal:
**Full size is unchanged, exactly 0.6451**, because a rotation keeps every full-size cosine (the same trick the toy in lesson 3 used). At 64 dims the score rises only from 0.484 to 0.502 (mean of 3 seeds, 5 epochs), and at 16 dims from 0.158 to 0.184.

A rotation can only move information between coordinates. It cannot create information the encoder never computed, so this trained rotation gains only a little.

blocks.code:
lin = torch.nn.Linear(384, 384, bias=False)
with torch.no_grad(): lin.weight.copy_(torch.eye(384))   # start at identity
rot = orthogonal(lin)            # torch.nn.utils.parametrizations: stays a rotation
opt = torch.optim.Adam(rot.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
DIMS = [384, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16]
for ep in range(5):
    perm = torch.randperm(len(A))
    for i in range(0, len(A) - 255, 256):           # batches of 256 pairs
        idx = perm[i:i + 256]
        za, zb = rot(A[idx]), rot(B[idx])            # frozen MiniLM vectors, rotated
        loss = 0
        for m in DIMS:                               # the Matryoshka sum, weight 1
            qa = F.normalize(za[:, :m], dim=1)
            qb = F.normalize(zb[:, :m], dim=1)
            loss = loss + F.cross_entropy(20 * qa @ qb.T, torch.arange(len(idx)))
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
# summed loss per batch fell from 2.12 (epoch 1) to 0.99 (epoch 5); about 20 s per run
blocks.caption: The training loop that ran (excerpt). A and B are precomputed, normalized MiniLM vectors of the NQ questions and passages.

blocks.title: SciFact nDCG@10 of MiniLM prefixes after a rotation (measured)

scenes.caption: 128 dims: 0.602, 0.598, 0.601, 0.609 and 0.632. PCA is the SVD rotation from lesson 1, fitted on the named vectors. Every rotation gives the same 0.645 at 384 dims.
64 dims: the MRL rotation gives 0.502, a random rotation 0.495. PCA fitted on the target corpus gives 0.559.
32 dims: 0.337, 0.383, 0.363, 0.326, 0.461. A random rotation beats the raw order and even the trained MRL rotation here: MiniLM's first coordinates are not special.
16 dims: 0.158, 0.168, 0.184, 0.131, 0.299. Only PCA on your own corpus clearly helps.

blocks.md:
**PCA** (principal component analysis) is the SVD option from lesson 1: rotate so the first axis carries the most variance of the stored vectors, the second the next most, and so on. Fitted on the SciFact abstracts themselves, it needs no labels and beat the MRL rotation at every size. Fitted on NQ passages it was mixed: ahead of the MRL rotation at 256 and 128 dims, tied at 64, behind at 32 and 16. Training the rotation on NLI pairs instead of NQ landed within noise of the NQ rotation (0.504 at 64 dims).

So for a model you cannot retrain, try a PCA rotation fitted on your own corpus before anything fancier. Matryoshka-Adaptor (lesson 3) is the trained version of this idea, with a small network and losses that keep the original similarities.

Check your splits. A first run trained the rotation on SciFact's own train claims and scored 0.713 at 64 dims, above the full vector's 0.645. Too good to be true: 181 of the 283 abstracts relevant to test claims are also cited by train claims. Dropping those pairs (624 of 919 remain) gave 0.504, the same as NQ.

Matryoshka training pays off when the encoder itself is trained with the nested loss on data that looks like your task. A prefix of a model trained for another task, or a post-hoc rotation of a frozen model, may hold up no better than an ordinary model. Read the card, then measure at the size you plan to serve.

blocks.question: A model card does not mention Matryoshka, you cannot retrain the model, and your index format needs 64-dim float vectors instead of 384. What should you try first?
options: Keep the first 64 coordinates: every model puts the important information first
Retrain it with MatryoshkaLoss on NLI pairs, because the loss works on any data
Fit PCA on your own corpus vectors, rotate, keep the first 64 dims, and measure on labeled queries
Learning a rotation is useless, because it changes the full-size scores
blocks.explain: In this lab a PCA rotation fitted on the target corpus took MiniLM from 0.484 to 0.559 at 64 dims with no labels. Raw prefixes of an ordinary model carry no guarantee, retraining on NLI data shapes prefixes for the wrong task, and a rotation leaves every full-size cosine exactly as it was.

blocks.question: Why did the NLI Matryoshka twin show no clear prefix advantage on SciFact, while it did on STS?
options: Its nested loss shaped the prefixes for NLI-style similarity, and SciFact asks a different question that neither NLI model answers well
Matryoshka models only work on images
SciFact abstracts are longer than 768 tokens, so the prefixes overflow
The twin was evaluated without re-normalizing its prefixes
blocks.explain: The loss keeps the training task's notion of similarity in the prefixes. On STS, the task family the pair was trained for, the twin kept 98.37% at 64 dims vs 96.46%. On out-of-domain retrieval, where both start weak (0.373 and 0.354), the prefixes kept 51.5% and 54.0%. Both runs re-normalized the prefixes.

lessons.title: Build it: pick a serving size and run a two-stage search on SciFact

blocks.md:
Now the full workflow on real data with nomic-embed-text-v1.5, a model trained for prefixes. The plan:

1. Encode the corpus and queries **once** at full size, 768 dims.
2. Score every combination of kept dims (768 down to 64) and precision (float32, int8, binary) on SciFact, and pick the smallest setting within your quality tolerance.
3. Try two-stage search: shortlist $K$ documents cheaply, rerank them with the full float vectors, and sweep $K$.
4. Express the same search in a database.

In this run, encoding the 300 claims and 5,183 abstracts took about 920 seconds on 2 CPU threads of one laptop (up to 512 tokens each); expect different times on other hardware. Every later step reuses those vectors.

blocks.code:
m = SentenceTransformer("nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5", trust_remote_code=True)
m.max_seq_length = 512
Q = m.encode(["search_query: " + q for q in claims])        # (300, 768)
D = m.encode(["search_document: " + d for d in abstracts])  # (5183, 768)

ln = lambda x: (x - x.mean(1, keepdims=True)) / np.sqrt(x.var(1, keepdims=True) + 1e-5)
n = lambda x: x / np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1, keepdims=True)
DL, QL = ln(D), ln(Q)                # the card's layer norm, on the full vector
for k in [768, 512, 256, 128, 64]:
    Dp, Qp = n(DL[:, :k]), n(QL[:, :k])       # slice, then re-normalize
    scores = Qp @ Dp.T                         # cosine; rank and compute nDCG@10
# int8: quantize_embeddings(Dp, precision="int8", calibration_embeddings=Dp)
# decode: lo, hi = Dp.min(0), Dp.max(0); x = (codes + 128) * (hi - lo) / 255 + lo
# binary: bits = Dp > 0, score = minus the Hamming distance
blocks.caption: Encode once, derive every size. Run in a scratch venv with sentence-transformers 3.3.1, because the model's custom code failed under transformers 5. Scores were ranked with NumPy.

blocks.title: SciFact nDCG@10 by kept dims and precision (nomic v1.5, this run)

scenes.caption: Full size, float32: 0.703 (3,072 bytes per vector). int8 scored on decoded values keeps it all (0.702); scored on raw codes it keeps 97.2% (0.683). Binary keeps 91.0% (0.640).
Down the float32 column the loss is gentle to 256 dims (0.6825, 97.1%), then speeds up: 0.642 at 128, 0.528 at 64. Decoded int8 tracks it at every size.
Binary losses compound with truncation: 0.478 at 256 dims (32 bytes), 0.171 at 64. Raw-code int8 also slides (89.1% at 64), but that is the scoring rule, not the storage.
Equal bytes, more dims at fewer bits wins. 256 B: 256-d int8 0.684 vs 64-d float32 0.528. 64 B: 512-d binary 0.581 vs 64-d int8 0.526 (decoded).

blocks.md:
**Choosing a single-stage setting.** Say you accept losing at most 3% of full nDCG@10, so the floor is 0.6821. With int8 scored on decoded values, the smallest setting that clears it is 256-d int8 (256 bytes, 0.684), a twelfth of the full float32 vector. Scored on raw codes, int8 would only clear it at 768 dims (768 bytes, 0.683), and float32 alone needs 256 dims (1,024 bytes, 0.6825). Tighten the tolerance to 1% (floor 0.6962) and the smallest is 512-d int8 decoded (512 bytes, 0.702).

Two lessons from this run. First, the binary losses grow fast as dims shrink, so truncation and binary compound their costs; int8 compounds only when raw codes are scored (97.2% of float32 at 768 dims, 89.1% at 64), while decoded int8 stays within 0.5% of float32 at every size (see below). Second, at equal bytes it paid to keep more dims at fewer bits. Both are specific to this model and dataset, which is exactly why you run the sweep.

**int8 calibration on prefixes.** The int8 column used per-dimension ranges computed on the stored, re-normalized prefixes, and scored by the plain dot product of the raw int8 codes, as the Hugging Face quantization study did; many engines instead decode the codes or correct for their offset. As a check, ranges taken from the full 768-d unit vectors were applied to the 64-d prefixes instead: they clipped 28.7% of the entries and nDCG@10 fell from 0.471 to 0.434. At 128 and 256 dims the same mistake clipped 15% and 5% of entries yet scored *higher* on raw codes (0.610 vs 0.591, 0.663 vs 0.638). That is an artifact of raw-code scoring: the codes are offset from zero, so their dot product is not proportional to cosine. Scored on decoded values (each code mapped back to its bucket's value), int8 with prefix ranges kept about 99.5% or more of float32 at every size, and full-vector ranges lost at every size below 768 (0.564 vs 0.644 at 128 dims). Calibrate on what you store, and rescore with decoded or float vectors.

blocks.prompt: For a shortlist of K = 50 that is then reranked with full float32 vectors, which first stage keeps more of the full search's top 10: 64-d float32 prefixes (256 bytes each) or 768-bit binary codes (96 bytes each)?
blocks.reveal:
**The binary codes, despite being smaller.** On average 84.5% of the full search's top 10 survive the 768-bit shortlist, against 70.8% for 64-d float32. After the rerank, nDCG@10 is 0.704 (equal to full search) against 0.673.

Here the sign of all 768 numbers carries more ranking information than 64 exact numbers. Matryoshka truncation is one lever, not always the best one.

blocks.title: Share of the full top 10 that survives the shortlist (measured)

scenes.caption: 64-d float32 shortlist: 39.6% at K = 10, 70.8% at 50, 91.3% at 200. After reranking, K = 200 gives nDCG@10 0.704, equal to full search.
256-bit binary (first 256 dims, 32 bytes): 54.4% at K = 50 and 90.9% at 500. Truncation plus binary needs a long shortlist.
768-bit binary (96 bytes): 84.5% at K = 50 and 91.4% at 100. From K = 50 on, the reranked nDCG@10 (0.703 to 0.706) matches full search.

blocks.caption: Multiply-adds per query for exact search: the 64-d shortlist with K = 200 is about 8.2x cheaper and matched full-search nDCG@10 here. A binary shortlist replaces the multiply-adds of stage 1 with XOR and bit counts.

blocks.code:
S_full = n(QL) @ n(DL).T                        # stage 2 scores, 768-d float32
bits_d, bits_q = DL > 0, QL > 0                 # 768-bit codes (96 bytes each)
ham = bits_q.astype(int) @ (~bits_d).T + (~bits_q).astype(int) @ bits_d.T
short = np.argsort(ham, axis=1, kind="stable")[:, :50]       # stage 1: K = 50
final = [c[np.argsort(-S_full[i, c])][:10] for i, c in enumerate(short)]
# nDCG@10: 0.7042 (full float32 search: 0.7032)
blocks.caption: Two-stage search in NumPy, binary shortlist then float rerank (excerpt of the script that produced the bars). In production the float vectors can live on disk: only K of them are read per query.

blocks.md:
**The same in Postgres.** The pgvector extension supports both patterns with expression indexes, per its README. Store the full 768-d vectors (after the layer norm); build an HNSW index on an expression such as the first 256 dims, `subvector(embedding, 1, 256)::vector(256)`, or the binary codes, `binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(768)`. A query orders by the same expression with `LIMIT K` in a subquery, then re-orders that shortlist by the full vector.

The cosine operator `<=>` divides by both lengths, so the prefix needs no separate re-normalization. The README also lists HNSW limits: up to 2,000 dims for `vector` and 64,000 for `bit`, so a 3,072-d vector must be shortened or cast to a smaller type before you can index it.

blocks.caption: Not run here: pgvector is not installed on this Mac. Adapted from the pgvector README's subvector re-ranking example. Its binary example swaps in binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(768) with bit_hamming_ops and the <~> operator.

blocks.md:
Vespa documents the same combination inside its embedder: the schema's tensor size picks the Matryoshka prefix and an int8 cell type packs it to sign bits, a first phase ranks by Hamming distance, and a second phase rescores with the float query. Its post cites mixedbread's report that mxbai-embed-large-v1 keeps about 90% of MTEB retrieval quality at 64 bytes per vector (512 dims as bits), and says rescoring with the float query lifts binary retrieval to 95 to 96% of float quality.

How ANN indexes such as HNSW, IVF and product quantization work, and where to keep the rescoring vectors, is beyond this course and nothing here depends on it; the separate *Vector search and ANN* course covers it.

Every query must be built exactly like the stored vectors: the same task prefix, the same layer norm, the same slice and the same bit rule. Each prefix size or precision you serve is its own index. In this run, skipping Nomic's layer norm changed nDCG@10 by at most 0.001, but other models and recipes may not be so forgiving.

blocks.question: Your 256-bit binary shortlist (first 256 dims) with K = 100 gives recall@10 of 0.790 after the float rerank, against 0.844 for full search. Which pair of fixes, with their costs, is right?
options: Rerank at more dims, or use float64 for the rerank: both cost nothing
Lower K to 50 to cut noise, or drop the rerank stage
Re-encode the corpus with a bigger model; there is no cheaper fix
Raise K to about 500 (more rerank work and float vectors read per query), or keep all 768 bits (96 instead of 32 bytes per vector in memory)
blocks.explain: The rerank already uses full vectors; it can only reorder what stage 1 found, so the fix is in stage 1. In this run, K = 500 restored recall@10 to 0.847 at 5x the rerank work, and 768-bit codes reached 0.847 at K = 100 for 3x the memory. A smaller K makes recall worse.

blocks.question: From the SciFact table, which single-stage setting gives the best nDCG@10 at 96 bytes per vector or less?
options: 64-d int8 (64 bytes)
768-d binary (96 bytes)
256-d binary (32 bytes)
512-d binary (64 bytes)
blocks.explain: 768-d binary scores 0.640 at 96 bytes; 512-d binary 0.581 at 64 bytes; 64-d int8 0.526 even when decoded (0.471 on raw codes); 256-d binary 0.478. Within this budget, fewer bits on all dims beat more bits on fewer dims for this model. Just over budget, 128-d int8 (128 bytes) reaches 0.644 decoded, a tie with 768-d binary.
